Breadcrumb Home Innovation & AI Models & research Gemini Models Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model Oct 28, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. The Founders Edition is a limited run of the Form Studio 1, available at launch while supplies last. It comes in signature Graphite or limited-edition Aqua, Violet, or Teal, and each printer displays a Founders Edition tag in its interface. Founders Edition perks include your first bottle of Alpha Resin for $29, a limited-edition Form Studio 1 plushie, and 25% off Form Now orders, up to $100 (US only). What is the Form Studio 1 used for? The Form Studio 1 is a desktop resin 3D printer for creators, designers, hobbyists, and studios who want professional-quality prints. Popular uses include tabletop miniatures and figurines, cosplay props, product design prototypes, art and sculpture, custom gifts, and small-batch parts for side businesses. What technology powers the Form Studio 1’s speed? The Form Studio 1 is an MSLA printer built on Low Force Display (LFD) technology. Its backlight unit uses 28 high-powered LEDs and collimating lenses to cure resin quickly and evenly across the entire build platform. How fast is the Form Studio 1? Most prints finish in under 2 hours (based on the 80th percentile print height of 53 mm at 100 µm layer height), and print time stays the same whether you print one part or a full build platform. With Alpha Fast Resin, the Form Studio 1 prints at up to 130 mm/hour. How accurate are parts printed on the Form Studio 1? XY dimensional tolerances are ±0.5% for 1–30 mm features, ±0.2% for 31–80 mm features, and ±0.03% for 81–150 mm features, with a lower limit of ±0.08 mm. A 35 µm pixel size and pre-tuned anti-aliasing deliver sharp detail, smooth surfaces, and parts that fit together as designed. How reliable is the Form Studio 1? In internal testing, the Form Studio 1 has shown print success comparable to Form 4, which achieved a 98.7% print success rate in independent testing . Full reliability testing for the Form Studio 1 is underway. How long does it take to learn to use the Form Studio 1? The system is designed to be highly intuitive. Most users can learn the full printing workflow in about 10 minutes. What software do I use to prepare prints for the Form Studio 1? PreForm , Formlabs’ free print preparation software, automatically orients models, generates supports, and slices your files, so you can optimize your layout and send jobs straight to the printer. Form Studio 1 is not compatible with third-party slicers or print preparation software. What materials can I use with the Form Studio 1? The Form Studio 1 supports six Alpha Resins developed specifically for it: Alpha Grey , Alpha White , Alpha Black , Alpha Clear , Alpha Fast , and Alpha Model . It also supports Tough 1500 Resin , Flexible 80A Resin , and True Cast Resin . Every supported material comes with validated print settings tested on the Form Studio 1, so you get reliable results without calibration or trial and error. Most other Formlabs resins are also compatible. These dispense automatically from the cartridge, but you'll need to tune your own settings and use the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank Pro . Print performance may be lower, and mechanical properties may differ from published values. You can also print third-party 405 nm resins using Open Material Mode. Automatic dispensing is disabled in this mode, so you'll pour resin manually and tune your own settings. What’s the difference between the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank and the Resin Tank Pro? The Form Studio 1 Resin Tank uses a film engineered for Alpha Resins, which gives faster prints and a better finish on supported surfaces. Some materials, including Tough 1500 Resin V2 and most third-party resins, contain ingredients that damage this film, so they require the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank Pro . Never print these materials in the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank. The film can degrade quickly and leak resin, which can damage your printer and leave a mess to clean up. How long do resin tanks last? Can I replace the tank film? Resin tanks are consumables, and their lifespan depends mainly on the number of layers printed and accumulated wear. With proper maintenance and Formlabs materials, Form Studio 1 resin tanks are designed to last more than 75,000 layers. The tank film can’t be replaced on either the Form Studio 1 Resin Tank or the Resin Tank Pro . What post-processing does the Form Studio 1 require? After printing, wash parts in IPA or Formlabs Resin Washing Solution to remove uncured resin, then UV-cure them to reach final mechanical properties. Form Studio Wash+Cure , or Form Wash and Form Cure , automate both steps. Can I monitor my prints remotely? Yes. A built-in camera lets you watch active prints, view time-lapses, and review your print history from the Form Mobile app or Formlabs Dashboard . Can the camera be disabled? Yes, in three ways: cover it with the included camera cap (in the accessories box or print your own from the preloaded print jobs), turn it off in the printer settings (also shown during onboarding), or unplug the camera cable to disconnect it completely. The camera and time-lapse are separate settings, so you can turn off time-lapse while keeping the camera on. Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments
body_text: DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work | Surge AI DAYJOB: Tax A benchmark for AI tax agents Blog benchmarks Off-the-Shelf Training experts Products Enterprise Research Careers Contact Login Menu Close THE SURGE AI BLOG DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work October 27, 2026 October 27, 2026 No items found. TL;DR Real-world tax work is messy. Instructions are incomplete, records conflict, and the most important problems aren't always the ones explicitly assigned. DAYJOB: Tax evaluates whether AI agents can handle that reality, taking ownership of a tax professional's work from an initial client request to a finished deliverable. Across 50 environments and 1,789 files, agents must navigate complex tax records, uncover issues clients may not know to raise, and make consequential judgments with incomplete information. Success requires more than tax knowledge and accurate calculations. It demands the initiative and professional judgment to figure out what needs to be done, investigate what matters, and deliver work that meets professional standards. ‍ LEADERBOARD HUGGING FACE Table of contents Case Study Llama Analysis of Individual writings Appendix Anna was planning to sell her condo. She had moved out in August 2024 and wanted to know whether closing in October 2026 or January 2027 would be better for taxes. An AI agent reviewed both options and correctly concluded that either date would satisfy the residence requirement for a tax break worth up to $250,000 in excluded gains. But it left out an important deadline. Under the usual rules, homeowners must have lived in a property for at least two of the five years before selling it to qualify for the exclusion. Because Anna moved out in August 2024, she would stop satisfying that requirement around the end of August 2027. If her sale was delayed beyond August 2027, she could lose eligibility. Across five attempts, Astra never identified the deadline. Opus identified it in all five attempts. The agent evaluated the proposed dates correctly, but its advice left Anna unaware of a deadline that could affect a major financial decision. A tax adviser should recognize consequential issues even when the client doesn't know to ask about them. This is the kind of professional judgment we're testing with DAYJOB: Tax , the latest addition to Surge AI's DAYJOB benchmark family . Introducing DAYJOB: Tax DAYJOB evaluates AI agents on professional tax assignments requiring specialized expertise, complex materials, and decisions that aren't fully specified in the initial instructions. Our earlier releases covered Healthcare and Finance. DAYJOB: Tax extends that work into tax preparation, compliance, and advisory services. The benchmark contains 50 environments across eight areas of tax practice. Agents receive client requests and supporting records, then produce tax returns, workpapers, technical reviews, or client advice. These assignments test professional judgment alongside tax knowledge, calculations, retrieval, and instruction following. Agents must decide what deserves investigation, resolve conflicting evidence, recognize when information is insufficient, and carry those decisions into their final work. Results: Leaderboard and Pareto Frontiers Claude Sonnet 5.5 leads with a 10.8% pass rate on the DAYJOB: Tax leaderboard , followed by Claude Fable 5.1 at 9.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 9.2%. We report pass@1 at a 95% rubric threshold. An attempt passes when it satisfies at least 95% of the task's criteria, which assess calculations, supporting evidence, consequential issues, and the completed deliverable. Performance versus cost We also compared model performance against average cost per trial. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 occupy the high-performance end of the measured Pareto frontier. The breadth of professional tax work DAYJOB: Tax covers eight areas, each requiring different rules, records, and expertise: Individual and family tax Small-business tax Partnerships Property and investments Estates, gifts, and trusts International tax Corporate transactions Tax review and disputes Some assignments require complete filing packages with supporting workpapers. Others ask agents to investigate transactions, review previous filings, or prepare advice about decisions clients haven't yet made. What's inside the assignments? The benchmark contains 1,789 workspace files , with a median of 30 per assignment and as many as 123. These include 1,487 PDFs, 117 Excel workbooks, 38 Word documents, and additional emails, images, CSVs, JSON records, and text files. The workspaces include filed and draft tax returns, K-1s, W-2s, IRS notices, general ledgers, payroll records, contracts, and correspondence. They also contain the less standardized evidence that tax professionals routinely work with. One assignment includes a photograph of a handwritten receipt for merchandise purchased for resale . The agent must read the item descriptions and amounts, reconcile them with spending records, and determine how the purchases affect inventory and cost of goods sold. Another assignment involves an industrial silo-services company whose client assumes it operates only in Alabama. But its field dispatch log shows crews working across five states . The job locations, crew sizes, and days on site provide evidence relevant to the company's multistate tax obligations. Other environments are similarly varied. One involves a cross-border household whose Polish employment and property records must be reconciled with cryptocurrency exchange exports, wallet histories, and historical purchase lots. Created and reviewed by tax experts DAYJOB tasks begin with real-world professional workflows. Tax experts turn these situations into realistic assignments, developing the supporting records, expected outcomes, and grading criteria. Each task undergoes a three-layer expert review for correctness, completeness, and solvability. Tax experts bring experience across corporate taxation, partnerships, individual returns, trusts, and multistate compliance. Their backgrounds include: Corporate and private-equity taxation: A tax attorney with over 10 years of experience at PwC, Deloitte, and Exxon, covering tax planning, compliance, audits, and controversy. Partnership and corporate taxation: A Baker Tilly Tax Director with experience at PwC, Moss Adams, and Windes, specializing in complex partnership allocations, consolidated corporate returns, REITs, and high-net-worth clients. Real estate and individual taxation: A tax professional with experience at Deloitte and EY, specializing in real-estate partnerships, individual taxation, and trusts. A retirement plan built on an unverified assumption A separating couple asked an AI agent how to divide their Roth IRA and 401(k). Opus 5.5 told them they weren't legally married and recommended keeping their accounts separate, with a cash payment to even out the balances. It opened one response: You aren't legally married, so neither account can be split without triggering taxes and penalties. But the couple's own records raised doubts about that conclusion. Although they now lived in Florida, where new common-law marriages generally aren't recognized, they had previously lived together in Texas and held a ceremony in Colorado. Texas recognizes informal marriages under certain conditions, and a valid marriage established elsewhere may remain valid in Florida. That distinction could change the tax consequences of dividing their retirement accounts. Across all five attempts, Opus based its recommendations around the assumption that the couple was unmarried , even when it acknowledged uncertainty. Astra recognized the need to verify their marital status in four of five attempts. One response advised: We first need to confirm your legal marital status. The client asked how to divide the accounts. The agent needed to establish whether they were married before recommending a course of action. The evidence that should have prompted that investigation was already in the files. Where DAYJOB: Tax fits Most existing tax benchmarks begin with a defined problem: a legal question to answer, a return to calculate, or missing taxpayer information to collect. These evaluations measure important capabilities, but much of a tax professional's work involves figuring out what the problem actually is. Clients provide incomplete instructions, records contain conflicting evidence, and consequential issues may never appear in the original request. DAYJOB tests whether agents can handle that end-to-end responsibility , including identifying issues the client overlooked, evaluating conflicting evidence, and deciding what needs to be done in the first place. TaxBench Can the model answer a difficult tax question? TaxBench evaluates 114 tax questions across multiple specialties, each with a defined problem and grading rubric. DAYJOB also asks whether the client asked the right question. Anna wants to compare two dates for selling her condo. Both satisfy the residence requirement for a tax exclusion, but does the agent warn her when that eligibility could expire? TaxCalcBench Can the model calculate an accurate return? TaxCalcBench evaluates tax-return accuracy against expected filing values, using realistic tax documents and taxpayer scenarios. DAYJOB also asks whether the underlying records actually support the tax treatment. A studio's ledger references an attached receipt, but the receipt is missing. Does the agent flag the missing evidence or incorrectly treat the reimbursement as verified? TaxLab Can the agent gather missing information and file correctly? TaxLab tests whether agents can question a simulated taxpayer, obtain missing information, and complete a federal individual tax return. DAYJOB extends that responsibility across the wider tax profession. The deliverable might be a partnership loss analysis, an estate return, a review of a disputed tax position, or a strategy letter. The central distinction is how much responsibility remains with the agent. DAYJOB evaluates whether agents can discover consequential issues, exercise professional judgment, and carry their findings through to a completed filing, review, or recommendation. What DAYJOB: Tax measures DAYJOB tests whether AI agents can take ownership of a professional assignment from start to finish. That means navigating messy records, identifying issues the client never raised, making sound judgments with incomplete information, and delivering work that meets professional standards. The results show how difficult that remains for frontier models. Even when agents can perform the individual steps, exercising professional judgment and reliably carrying out real-world tax workflows remain out of reach. Agents haven’t yet passed the audit. Download ZIP Claude Code burns ~15-20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line: a Bun preload that turns agent_summary off · by Flamerix AI, flamerix.ai · MIT Raw README.md Claude Code burns ~15–20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line. Here's how to turn it off by Flamerix AI · MIT License Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312; macOS reported working by others (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified ( BUN_OPTIONS=--preload ). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify. TL;DR Every ~30 seconds, Claude Code re-sends each background agent's full transcript to the model just to fill that agent's status line in the agents panel. no-agent-summary.js is a Bun --preload that stops that timer without modifying the Claude Code binary. curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~ /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js claude daemon stop --any BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " claude To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install . Contents The problem The fix (how it works) Which processes it touches Install Env Nuances Verify (after every update) Fail-open Effect Tested versions Why there is no setting for this Timeline (2026) Changelog License and disclaimer The problem Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default. The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself . query_source = agent_summary week before the hook 2 days after share of all Claude Code spend 16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 % share of all API requests 19.7 % , about 1 in 5 0 % part of that spend on Opus 96 % — input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 — Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate ( cost_usd ), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %. The fix (how it works) no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~70 lines of code). It wraps only the global setTimeout , the one the summary timer is armed through; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary . Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch . But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once. Which processes it touches The hook installs only inside Claude Code: Bun.main must be /$bunfs/root/cli (the compiled entry, the same on every row below) and process.execPath must be a Claude Code install. Any other bun , or a compiled Bun binary with another entry name, loads the file and does nothing. install channel (Linux, measured with claude --version ) process.execPath nix …/bin/.claude-wrapped npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/bin/claude.exe ( .exe on Linux too) npm platform package …/@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64/claude native installer ~/.local/share/claude/versions/<version> macOS and Windows are not measured; the hook installs there only if they produce these same shapes, and Verify step 1 tells you. One known pass-through: a foreign binary built with bun build --compile --outfile cli and renamed claude ; there, only timers whose callback carries an anchor change. Install Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path. Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. Write --preload=<path> , with = : BUN_OPTIONS reaches every bun on the machine, and with a space ( --preload <path> ) bun subcommands break ( bun install → error: Script not found "install" ). Claude Code reads both forms. One of: # ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/fish/config.fish set -gx BUN_OPTIONS " --preload=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js " # ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches # user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login) BUN_OPTIONS =-- preload =/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another, and also recognises the v2 space form): #! /bin/sh HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in * " --preload= $HOOK " * | * " --preload $HOOK " * ) ;; * ) export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload= $HOOK " ;; esac : " ${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG := ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR :-/ tmp} / no-agent-summary.log} " export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG exec /path/to/the/real/claude " $@ " Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has BUN_OPTIONS : claude daemon stop --any Env variable values effect CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE off (default), pass off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off . CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG file path, optional Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=global.setTimeout on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count. CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER file path, optional Overwritten on load with the preload active … line. Nuances Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any . Headless runs need it too: claude -p , cron, CI, editor integrations. Platform: Linux tested by us, macOS (darwin-arm64) reported working by others, Windows untested (see Which processes it touches ). npm --ignore-scripts : bin/claude stays a shell stub and Bun never starts, so the hook never runs. Upgrading from v2: overwrite the file in place, switch BUN_OPTIONS to the = form and restart the daemon. If both forms name the same path, bun loads it once. Two different paths (say an old copy kept beside the new one) both load: a second v3 copy is a no-op, but v2 has no such guard, so do not leave a v2 path in BUN_OPTIONS . A/B: CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the off result is the hook's doing. Background processes: daemon, pty host and bg-spare must carry --preload in their environment ( /proc/<pid>/environ on Linux); if not, restart the daemon. Verify (after every update) Preload loads: BUN_OPTIONS= " --preload= $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log Expect preload active mode=off … . No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute. Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log , run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, query_source = agent_summary should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode. Fail-open Matching is by source text : an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen: the log line or query-source id is renamed; the callback is passed via fn.bind(...) (no source in toString ) or another wrapper; the strings move to a shared constant outside the callback; the timer moves off the global setTimeout ( setInterval , require("timers") , timers/promises , a scheduler loop). So re-run Verify after every update. Effect We run it under every Claude Code process on our machine (2.1.301). Since then there have been zero agent_summary requests, and no other side query grew to take its place. Subagents, background agents, forked skills and background sessions run normally; only the summary fork is skipped. Visible change: the per-agent panel status stops updating; SDK task_progress has no summary . Overhead: one Function.prototype.toString per distinct timer callback, cached in a WeakMap . claude --version : ~10 ms → ~17 ms (one measurement). Tested versions Linux x64 binary from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 (its sha256 equals the native installer's manifest.json checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: claude -p --model haiku with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1 , one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting [AgentSummary] Forking in --debug-file . The two v3 rows are this script, re-run on 2026-10-29. The rows below them were measured with v2. version published sha256 static summary forks in a ~2.5-min agent run: no hook / hook pass / hook off notes 2.1.312 v3 2026-10-27 4f4178ce41d8 OK 5 / 6 / 0 the pass run took 232 s on a loaded machine, so one more 30 s tick fit; off with the gist file itself: 0 2.1.301 v3 2026-10-15 bc1aad9982c7 OK 5 / 5 / 0 run through the Nix-packaged binary rather than the npm one 2.1.312 2026-10-27 4f4178ce41d8 OK 5 / 5 / 0 latest on 2026-10-28; interactive: 6 no hook, 0 off 2.1.310 2026-10-23 b73676430af1 OK 5 / 5 / 0 2.1.308 2026-10-22 356733f185fa OK 5 / 6 / 0 stable on 2026-10-28; the pass run's agent took 9 steps instead of 8 2.1.301 2026-10-15 bc1aad9982c7 OK 5 / 5 / 0 same with earlier hook builds; interactive off also 0; in daily use since 2026-10-26, 0 agent_summary requests in telemetry 2.1.280 2026-09-22 1e08503dbdf3 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) interactive: -p cannot enable summaries on this version. The agent sat at a permission prompt, so later timers skipped the unchanged transcript 2.1.257 2026-09-01 9a64bda9d872 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) same as 2.1.280 5 / 5 / 0 = the fork happens on this version, merely loading the hook changes nothing, and off removes it. Reported by others platform version checked by macOS 26.7.1, native darwin-arm64, bun 1.4.4 2.1.312 static: the 3–5 words prompt, the timer (30 s, clamped 30–240 s), no off switch; live: the preload loads, and an interactive session with a background subagent logged summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) . Token numbers not checked (no OTEL export) lostsock , HN, 2026-10-29 On claude -p : headless runs don't arm the summary timer by default. Our live tests set CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1 for that reason. The default-on overhead is in interactive sessions with background agents. Why there is no setting for this The documented switch only turns it on. The SDK option agentProgressSummaries defaults to false , but in the bundle it is one term of an OR, and every code path that writes it sets true . So false changes nothing, and the undocumented CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES can only enable summaries too. The interval belongs to the server. It comes from a per-model-family server flag and is clamped to 30–240 s. The default is already the minimum, and no value disables the timer. The obvious env vars miss. DISABLE_NON_ESSENTIAL_MODEL_CALLS , which some packagers set, does not occur in the binary at all. CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 do stop it, but only by taking fork subagents or background agents with it. The prompt cache makes it cheaper, not cheap. About 98 % of these calls re-read the transcript from cache; the ~2 % that hit a cold cache carry over a third of its cost. Cost tools that read transcripts don't see it. These requests are not written to the session logs on disk ( #104358 ); only the OpenTelemetry export shows them. The docs section on background token usage doesn't list it either, while Agent View's row summaries are documented as a Haiku-class model refreshing every few minutes. A cheaper variant already exists, switched off. 2.1.310 ships a short mode: about 2k tokens of notes instead of the full transcript, optionally written by a smaller model. The default is still the full transcript, and only server flags can change it. Timeline (2026) version (published) what changed 2.1.32 (Feb 5) the code first appears; dead in public builds 2.1.72 (Mar 9) reachable as an SDK opt-in 2.1.117 (Apr 21) reachable in the interactive CLI behind the fork gate or a server rollout ≤ 2.1.220 (Jul 24) forked skills are always summarized 2.1.232 (Aug 13) on by default for interactive background agents 2.1.300 (Oct 14) interval becomes server-tunable, 30–240 s 2.1.310 (Oct 23) the cheaper short mode lands, switched off In our telemetry its weekly share of spend went from 3.5–7 % in July (the fork gate was already open for us) to 7.3 % and then 11.8 % in the week we picked up 2.1.233, and to about 16 % by mid-October. Changelog docs — first macOS report (darwin-arm64, 2.1.312) added to Tested versions . Thanks to lostsock . v3 — --preload=<path> everywhere (the space form broke bun subcommands); the hook installs only inside Claude Code ( Bun.main plus process.execPath , see Which processes it touches ); a second load in the same process is a no-op. title: AlpineBSD
body_text: AlpineBSD wiki AlpineBSD packages source mailing lists irc › ai policy › art › contributing/ › installation/ › non free Welcome to AlpineBSD! AlpineBSD is an operating system based on the NetBSD kernel with a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux and the objective of making it possible to use as little AI-generated software as possible . There is no LLM output included in the base system or main package repository ( AlpineBSD AI policy ). AlpineBSD is a work in progress . There is currently no installer available. For the adventurous, a very high-level installation guide is available here . Compared to NetBSD AlpineBSD ships the NetBSD kernel, libc, and essential platform-specific tools like mount . NOTICE : The NetBSD kernel has spotty hardware support, much less so than Linux. You cannot necessarily expect AlpineBSD to work on any random computer you have lying around. Consult the NetBSD supported hardware list for more information, particularly for laptops. Compared to Alpine Linux AlpineBSD ships with the apk-tools package manager and busybox, and a slightly more GNU-oriented userspace, preferring e.g. GNU make over BSD make. AlpineBSD is not a fork of Alpine Linux, its package collection is original (though many packages are ultimately based on aports). Alpine Linux uses the OpenRC init system. Currently, AlpineBSD uses s6 and we intend to add OpenRC as an alternative. Powered by werc and AlpineBSD • AlpineBSD logo by tomosh

title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
body_text: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates ← Main Page Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates 28th October 2026 Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates. Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again. Meanwhile, dozens of other projects , many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago. Why does this matter? Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make. For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted. To check whether your git is affected, run: git ls-remote https://git-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with. To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates. git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/galadran/emudhra-git-test A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED . A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves. You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example: git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/Homebrew/brew curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run: curl https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ A certificate error means curl is protected. What should Apple do? Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework. Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem . What can developers do in the meantime? The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix. Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk. Site published by Dennis Jackson . This site is the work of many contributors from the community. The source is on GitHub and PRs are welcome. Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 .

title: A Health Update
body_text: A Health Update • furbo.org Skip to content furbo.org furbo.org furbo.org info About Me I'm Craig Hockenberry and this is where I write for the web. I make apps and run websites . You can learn more about me , view my rÃ©sumÃ© , check out my source code , or follow me . Search for: Recent Writing A Health Update TipKit for the Real World Spotlight: Not Right Pico Names Your Mac and a Canon Printer The Year That Kicked My Ass Tahoe Electron Detector One Size Does Not Fit All FB19914338 UITabAccessory Backward Compatibility Archives 2026 2025 2024 2023 2022 2021 2020 2019 2018 2017 2016 2015 2014 2013 2012 2011 2010 2009 2008 2007 RSS in XML or JSON © 2026 Craig Hockenberry All rights reserved A Health Update I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier. You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative. My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope. Lovely to look at, less lovely to lie on. Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate . There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back. It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react. The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine. That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do. Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab . Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer. The first effect I noticed was in my tastebuds: everything I put in my mouth had a slightly metalic taste, so my eating habits changed. My beloved morning coffee was replaced by tea, food needed a lot less salt, and I started eating a blander diet (cottage cheese with berries remains a favorite). Some people experience nausea and other gastric issues: luckily, I avoided that. I also didn’t have any hair loss, but my normally thick and curly hair lost its body and became lifeless: an external expression of what was happening to me internally. As someone who’s always been active and strong, the biggest overall effect of chemo was losing muscle mass and suffering from overall fatigue. It felt very strange to be weak. I was on a 28 day cycle for my infusions: during the first week I got pumped full of chemicals and then spent three weeks letting my body process them. One of the things they gave me with the infusion on a Tuesday was a dose of steroids that gives the body a boost during the initial onslaught. But by the weekend, that wore off and I felt like shit. It usually took until the middle of the second week before I started feeling human again. I didn’t lose my appetite, but I wasn’t eating more than normal. The problem was my metabolism was working overtime and my calorie intake didn’t adjust. I lost 50 pounds over the course of a couple of months and eventually got to the point where I was having five meals a day. Too bad it all tasted bad. This could also be a graph of my happiness. One thing that I did to fight my diminished capacity was a daily walk. Anyone who exercises regularly knows that there are always plenty of reasons to avoid it: you didn’t sleep well, you have an important project to finish, or you’re sore from a previous workout. When you’re doing chemo, add feeling like absolute shit to that list. I still had nerve damage in my spine, so my “walk” was more like a shuffle. Thankfully my wife found some awesome walking sticks to aid with my balance. They are clearly labelled “Not A Medical Device” but they are my most important medical device. Winter sunsets, exercise, and walking sticks are good medicine. My daily exercise was just like any gym workout: dread at the start, joy at the end. Sometimes there wasn’t much behind that joy: at my lowest point, a walk around the block on flat ground got my heart rate up to 160 bpm. Breathtaking, literally. That low point was in March. In the week following my infusion, where I was already feeling like crap, I came down with a type of pneumonia that affects people with weakened immune systems. I had no strength and my blood oxygen level plummeted below 90%. Getting from the living room to the kitchen for a drink of water felt like running a marathon, and then my Apple Watch pinged to inform me that I was having an episode of atrial fibrillation. It was a lot and I honestly had thoughts of “is this how it ends?” Thankfully, antibiotics battled the pneumonia quickly and the chemo effects subsided. My doctor offered to skip the next cycle of chemotherapy, but I decided to push on. There is only one way to be done with a thing. Throughout all of the infusions, the nerve damage that occurred before the lymphoma discovery didn’t improve. As I said above, my gait and balance were severely compromised: going up and down stairs was particularly challenging. The tingling sensations on my backside and numbness near my abdomen became a bigger concern with each passing month. It wasn’t getting better and I feared it was a permanent condition. I finished the last of my infusions in May and my body slowly started to recover. Food started tasting better, and my strength and stamina started to return. My daily walks got longer: first a quarter of a mile, then half a mile, then a mile, and then something fantastic happened. At the end of a walk around our local state park , I went to grab something in the car glovebox. As I did this, I tilted my head forward and the back of my legs lit up with a feeling I had never felt. Something was changing in my spine: and after a couple of weeks it was clear that this was a sign that the nerves were fixing themselves. Our guess is that the chemotherapy infusions, which attack white blood cells and other parts of the blood that aid in recovery, had retarded the healing in my nervous system. Now that my body had a chance to repair itself, it was. I can now go up and down stairs without hanging on for dear life. I’m able to walk without aid, but I still like my walking sticks for longer outings since they let me push myself harder. I’ve also started working out in a gym with a trainer: I told him about my stair issues, and now he has me doing them backwards and by hopping on all fours. I am so happy to look like a doofus, and for the continued improvement I’m seeing with exercise. My regained ability to walk and a stronger immune system allowed me to leave the house. My first night away from home was a short trip to Topanga Canyon to celebrate an August birthday: All hail the sunflower goddess! After that successful trip, we took a short boat ride to have a nice lunch and look at some kelp . It felt so good to be able to do normal things again. A trip to visit The Blue Forest One lingering part of my life that hasn’t been reestablished is swimming. All the chemotherapy that has been put into my body has been through a port catheter : a small device under my skin that hooks directly into my carotid artery. Getting an infection there would be a very bad thing, and water increases that risk: be it from ocean water full of living organisms or a swimming pool that kids pee in. With the current El NiÃ±o conditions, that’s been a hard thing: the water is warm and “interesting”. My new gym also has a beautiful Olympic-sized pool for lap swimming. I’m happy to be in this hospital bed doing a final stint of chemotherapy because when I’m done, the port is removed. This last procedure is to make sure there is no lymphoma in my brain fluids: not a difficult or dangerous treatment and the side effects are minimal. But it does require close monitoring because of the high dosages involved. In six weeks, I’ll be done and spend the winter in that heated pool so that I can finally swim in my beloved Pacific next summer. The buoys are still there, even though the high surf this summer knocked one out! Last year was hard, and it got worse over time. This year has also been hard, but it’s gotten better with each passing month. For that I’m grateful. I’m also grateful for my wife Lauren: it’s impossible to imagine making it through all of this without her help, support, and encouragement. The silver lining in all this strife is that it’s made our relationship much stronger. Thanks sweetie! As with my previous account , there’s an unwanted coda. No matter how hard I try, there’s a complication at the happy ending! I had typed up everything above as the doctors and nurses prepared me for the first dose of methotrexate. It takes a while for your blood’s pH level to reach a point where the treatment is safe, so I spent much of the day lying in bed, peeing into urine cups, reminiscing about my year, and typing. Around 10:30 PM, the medication was in my brain and I was trying to wind down for the night (easier said than done when part of the regimen includes steroids). While scrolling through Tapestry , I noticed quite a few posts about a newly announced PHP vulnerability. This caught my attention because we use it for our blogs, an ad server, delivering Kickstarter rewards, and a bunch of other small things. (This is the point where family that doesn’t understand what I do for a living continues to not understand what I do for a living.) It quickly became apparent that this was a big deal and something that could allow an attacker access to our server. I had to shut things down before my brain shut down. Thank goodness the steroids held out. After a couple of hours, I had blocked access to PHP processes in every nook & cranny of our server. After sending a quick message to our Slack explaining how everything was broken, I collapsed. The next day started with a head and server that were barely working. Our server was out of LTS, so the first order of business was to get it back onto the latest version of Ubuntu using hospital WiFi. It was a good thing my heart rate and blood pressure were being closely monitored. (Thank goodness for Lish , which proved to be immune to hospital IT shutting down my ssh connection to accept terms & conditions every few hours. There’s also a “I should have my head examined” joke in here somewhere.) If you noticed that the Iconfactory sites were kinda broken last week, now you know why. It’s because I was kinda broken last week. Now I’m finishing this post from a comfy chair on our deck. Typing into the latest version of WordPress and PHP. And I couldn’t be happier. Written on October 28th, 2026 for Miscellaneous Latest

body_text: CNC Stone Carving - Carmelite Gothic Carmelite Monks of Wyoming Gothic Gothic Why Gothic Architecture? Gothic Theory Methods for Constructing Gothic Architecture Gothic Elements CNC Stone Carving Stone Setting Resources for Gothic Architecture Our Design Ancient Carmelite Architecture Carmelite Gothic Monastery Gothic Church Design Chapter House Refectory Building Hermitage Porter’s Lodge Progress The Monks CNC Stone Carving Home » CNC Stone Carving CNC Stone Carving In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place. However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange. To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head. (The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.) CNC carving of a Gothic pinnacle by the Carmelite Monks CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today.  The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God. CNC Programing of a Gothic pinnacle by a Carmelite Monk What is a CNC machine CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention. Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process. CNC stone cutting blade and bits used by the Carmelite Monks Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings! CNC lathe and spindle at work carving stone for Carmelite Monks Prussiani CNC machines The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs. The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving.  Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task!  Here’s a little story to illustrate.  For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills.  We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning.  The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine.  Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the inside of the CNC milling area.  After the shock settled, we proceeded to analyze what had happened.  It turns out there was a mistake in the particular batch of code the machine had read and followed that night.  At the very end of each window sill, after it had completely finished carving, the code told the CNC machine to repeatedly pound down into the top of the sill, almost as if it was a giant fist.  The stones didn’t stand a chance, but that same machine is still carving stones to this day, almost a decade later. The Carving Process The process of carving stone with a CNC is a digital workflow.  The ornate pieces covered in foliage, the statues, the gargoyles, and many other distinct Gothic elements begin with the artist, the head carver.  He sculpts the various flowers and leaves using a 3d modeling program in a process much similar to molding a ball of clay.  It still requires a great deal of artistic talent, but there is a major advantage to this work in a computer, the Undo button!  The artist can experiment with an almost infinite number of designs to find the one most suited to the space.  And with the ability to visualize the pieces in a full model of the church, there is no longer any guesswork as to what the finished building will look like.  The Brother artist carving in mudbox for the Carmelite Monks Gothic Once the artist has finished a particular sculpture it is passed on to the actual stone carvers, the CNC programmers.  The programmers take the 3d model into a CAM program, which stands for computer aided machining, and create the toolpaths that the CNC machine will use to carve the actual stones.  Utilizing a large arsenal of tooling and methods they gradually carve the stone down to the finished piece.  They do their best to transform the stone block they start with to as close a resemblance of the artist’s model as possible, similar to the way stone carvers have historically used a pointing machine to transfer measurements from a plaster model into stone.  At the same time they have to juggle a wide array of concerns, from which tools to use depending on speed and finish, to how to keep the stone from moving, to avoiding collisions between the cnc and the stone, or even other stones they might be carving at the same time.  This is a lot to keep track of, but if done well, it will quickly bear fruit.  It is extremely rewarding to see the keystrokes and mouse clicks of a computer turn into not only a finished product, but an ornately carved part of a Gothic church, a place God will be loved for centuries to come. Finally, once all of that Gcode (the programming language of a CNC machine) is ready, it is handed over to the sawyers, who operate the CNC machines themselves, as well as the various other saws that prepare the stone blocks for carving.  The sawyers are the “boots on the ground” guys and keep a clear line of communication open with the programmers to ensure that everything runs smoothly.  They carefully follow the layouts and tooling lists the programmers prepare for each piece as they set up the stones for carving, set reference points so the machines can locate each stone, and monitor it as it carves.  They are constantly keeping a watchful eye to ensure that everything goes smoothly.  There is a symbiotic relationship between the sawyers and the programmers as the work of each is essential to the successful completion of each stone.  The Monk Sawyers setting up a table to be Carved for the CNC The sawyers also operate the wire saws and bridge saws, cutting each stone to either be carved into something more ornate, or to go straight into the wall.  The wire saw, a simpler type of 2 axis cnc itself, can cut simple profiles, including any straight piece, such as columns and the straight parts of window surrounds.  The sawyer, using the wire saw, will take a large slab of stone and sometimes cut even 20 or 30 different smaller stones out of it; looking similar to pieces from a cookie cutter.  This frees up the 5 axis CNC machines to focus on the more ornate pieces, and is also significantly faster. The monk Wire sawyer puts in plastic shims to support the cut pieces. On the right is the finished product of the wire saw awaiting the denesting of the profiled stones There are many different facets to the art and science of stone carving today and only a few have been touched on here.  Pneumatic chisels and hand carving certainly have a valuable role to play, as well as a multitude of other methods not discussed here.  The learning curve to dive into such a work is indeed daunting, the workload intimidating, but the fruit of it will stand for centuries to come.   Latest Posts Chapter House First Look Carving a Gothic Finial Coming Soon! title: The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds PCBs on demand
body_text: CircuitHub - Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen Capabilities PCB Stackups Design Rules Certifications ProtoBoard Case Studies Careers FAQ Blog Podcast About Us Careers Press Contact Sign In Sign Up support@circuithub.com +1 617-401-0319 Sign In Sign Up Menu G Blog All News Updates Tips Community Back to Site Back to the site Case study Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen News Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen Andrew on October 26, 2026 For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand. The problem Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked. Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it. Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops. What The Grid is The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it. Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines. It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid. What it means for a real board To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address. Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median. So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165. It's not a prototype The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers. What's next Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. This year we will 5x capacity, with another big jump coming in 2027. The longer-term goal hasn't changed since we started: make building hardware as fast as designing it. Electronics manufacturing left the West because it couldn't be automated at the volumes most companies need. The Grid shows it can. If you want to help rebuild the Western electronics supply chain, we're hiring . And if you have a board to build, get an instant quote .
