Our mission is to ensure the world safely makes the transition through transformative AI. Log in Claude.ai Claude console © 2026 Anthropic PBC

title: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
body_text: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course Subscribe Sign in Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch. Sebastian Raschka, PhD Oct 24, 2026 366 14 37 Share I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. The companion book These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. The videos As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. 1. Motivation and code setup The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. Topics covered The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses On the benefits of learning through code implementations The scope of this video series Installing Python dependencies Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment Watch video 1 · Setup instructions 2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. Topics covered Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code 3. Building a verifier for evaluation and reinforcement learning In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Topics covered Intro to verifiers and how they fit into LLM evaluation methods (other methods are covered in the book’s appendix) Reusing answer verification as a reward signal for RLVR (more on that in chapter 6) The verifier flow, including extracting final answers, normalizing answers and checking mathematical equivalence Building an answer grader and an evaluation loop for MATH-500 Comparing base and reasoning models on MATH-500 Watch video 3 · Chapter 3 code 4. Inference-time scaling: sampling and self-consistency Now we explore ways to improve answers while keeping the model weights fixed. But before implementing specific inference-scaling techniques, we first implement methods to generate diverse answers from the same prompt (this is standard practice in proprietary LLM chatbots, such as ChatGPT). Concretely, we implement temperature scaling, multinomial sampling, and top-p filtering to generate diverse responses. Then we combine multiple responses through self-consistency, using majority voting over their final answers. We also examine the tradeoff between answer accuracy and the extra computation needed to generate more candidates. Topics covered Comparing how additional compute benefits model performance during training and during inference A gentle intro to inference-scaling through chain-of-thought prompts Implementing temperature scaling and multinomial sampling to generate diverse answers Adding top-p filtering to control the quality of the diverse answers Combining candidate answers through self-consistency, one of the most popular inference scaling techniques Evaluating MATH-500 accuracy against the cost of additional inference compute Watch video 4 · Chapter 4 code 5. Inference-time scaling: scoring and self-refinement Building on the previous video, we implement scoring functions to compare multiple answers generated from the same prompt. We can also use these scoring methods to break ties in self-consistency (covered in the previous lecture). The scoring methods covered here include computing token and sequence log probabilities (this will also be relevant in the later reinforcement learning chapters). We then implement a self-refinement loop in which the model critiques an answer and attempts a revision. The evaluation lets us check how useful those additional steps are for our model. Topics covered Using scoring functions for comparing multiple answers and breaking ties Implementing a simple heuristic scorer Computing token probabilities and sequence likelihoods (also relevant for the following lectures) Using log probabilities for improved numerical stability Building a self-refinement loop for generating critiques and revised answers Evaluating self-refinement on MATH-500 Watch video 5 · Chapter 5 code 6. Reinforcement learning: implementing GRPO for RLVR In this lecture, we move on to implementing a training technique called Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We first implement a simplified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), generate groups of responses, score them with our verifier, and use their relative rewards for the model weight updates during training. Topics covered Generating reasoning traces and understanding the relationship between answer lengths and problem-solving abilities Discussion and comparison of two important LLM post-training methods: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Turning verifier scores into rewards and relative advantages Computing sequence log probabilities and a simplified GRPO loss Assembling the training loop with logging and checkpoint saves Evaluating checkpoints and checking training stability and memory needs Watch video 6 · Chapter 6 code 7. Reinforcement learning: tracking, clipped policy ratios, and KL terms Now that we implemented the training loop in the previous lecture, we can revisit it and analyze the training runs in more detail. Concretely, this video adds more training metrics for inspection and analysis, including entropy and advantage statistics, clipped policy ratios, KL loss term values, and formatted rewards. We then review the training logs and evaluation results to understand what these additions do and whether additions such as clipped policy ratios and KL loss terms are helpful. Topics covered Running longer training experiments and interpreting their logs Tracking advantages and entropy to understand training behavior Implementing clipping in the policy loss and analyzing its effects Adding a KL loss term and discussing reward hacking Understanding limitations of the simplified KL formulation Implementing format rewards and conditioning them on answer correctness Comparing checkpoints on MATH-500 and exploring further GRPO research Watch video 7 · Chapter 7 code 8. Distilling a reasoning model Finally, we explore another way to train a small reasoning model, that is, learning from answers generated by a stronger (and bigger) teacher model. We discuss different forms of distillation, prepare reasoning data, and implement the supervised training loop. We finish this lecture and course by evaluating the distilled model on MATH-500 and comparing the results. This rounds out the series with an alternative to developing reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning. Topics covered Comparing the different combination and approaches to distillation, including soft and hard distillation, and on-policy and off-policy distillation Creating and collecting teacher-generated answers for the MATH dataset (using DeepSeek R1) Preparing the distillation dataset, including tokenization and training/validation/test splits Computing answer-token log probabilities and understanding the cross-entropy loss Implementing supervised training and tracking training and validation losses Evaluating checkpoints on MATH-500 and comparing distillation results Watch video 8 · Chapter 8 code Final words As you watch these lectures, I encourage you to pause occasionally and try a small experiment of your own if something interesting comes to mind. For example, feel free to change the sampling settings, inspect a few failed answers, or try variations of different ideas similar to the suggestions in the exercises. And if you would like the full written walkthrough, figures, and exercises alongside the videos, you can find Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) at Manning and Amazon . Thanks for reading and supporting Ahead of AI. I am taking a short break to regenerate, and I look forward to being back with the next round of LLM research articles next month. In the meantime, happy viewing and tinkering! 366 14 37 Share Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Bachu Adharsh Kumar 5d Liked by Sebastian Raschka, PhD Reasoning models explained from scratch is what students need. Do you think a small model can show real reasoning gains on a normal laptop? Reply Share 2 replies by Sebastian Raschka, PhD and others Shamik 4d Liked by Sebastian Raschka, PhD Thank you for the amazing content, as always. Now i have something to look forward to during the holiday season. Love the picture at the end. Happy regeneration. Reply Share 12 more comments... Top Latest Discussions No posts Ready for more? title: The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI
body_text: The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI - Jan van den Berg Jan van den Berg Home About Quotes Search 🇳🇱 RSS The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI 27 October 2026 Last weekend I watched four people desperately trying to get a laptop to connect to a screen. I was happily observing their efforts, with zero intent to join in. But someone nudged me: can't you have a look at it? My reply: "Haha sorry no! My experience is that adding more people will not solve this problem any quicker". I was of course -- indirectly -- referring to Brooks's Law: "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." It was formulated by computer scientist Frederick P. Brooks Jr. in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, based on his experience managing the IBM OS/360 project. However I got to thinking. Does this still hold up in the age of AI agents and LLMs? At first glance, you’d think no. The traditional bottlenecks -- onboarding time, endless stand-ups, and office politics -- disappear overnight. An AI agent is up to speed in milliseconds and doesn't demand a coffee break. But when you look closer, and the law hasn't vanished. It just mutated. The famous "Baby Problem" remains: nine agents still can’t deliver a baby in one month. Sequential tasks are still sequential. Overhead hasn't disappeared; it shifted: instead of managing people, you are now managing agents. Someone still needs to define "done", review the code, catch hallucinations, and stitch the pieces together. That someone is you. Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop. Maybe the 2026 update to Brooks’s Law should be: "Adding agents to a project with unclear requirements gets you the wrong answer faster." ⬅ Previous post Interview with Ondřej Surý in the Atlantic Next post ➡ Going to the top on Hacker News © 2026 Jan van den Berg

title: A Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting
body_text: The Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting Skip to main content Search This Blog Metadata On distributed systems broadly defined and other curiosities. The opinions on this site are my own. The Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting Get link Facebook X Pinterest Email Other Apps - October 26, 2026 I have come to suspect that to most people thinking is painful. Some of us are addicted to thinking. Some of us find it a necessity. Johnny enjoyed it. I even have the suspicion that he enjoyed almost nothing else. -- Edward Teller, eulogizing John von Neumann I listened to Ananyo Bhattacharya's " The Man from the Future: The Visionary Life of John von Neumann " in my car during the many commute hours Bay Area traffic afforded me. I thought I should share the Johnny phenomena here. I knew about von Neumann being a very influential mathematician/scientist/engineer but the full list still left me bedazzled. In his 53 years of life (1903-1957), von Neumann seeded so many fields. Every time there was an important discovery in physics, mathematics or computation, John von Neumann was there. Set theory and the foundations of mathematics. The mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics. Operator algebras (still called von Neumann algebras). Ergodic theory. Game theory. Expected utility theory (which is the foundation of most of modern mathematical economics). The Monte Carlo method. The stored-program computer architecture that every machine you have ever touched is built on. Numerical weather prediction. Fault-tolerant computing. Self-reproducing automata (cellular automata), and arguably, the logical structure of molecular biology, four years before Watson and Crick. There is also, unfortunately, the implosion lens for the Nagasaki bomb, and a decade of hawkish nuclear strategy. Early years At six, Janos (the OG hungarian name for Johnny) could divide eight-digit numbers in his head and hold a conversation in ancient Greek. He later added Latin, French, German, English, and Yiddish.  The rumor was that he remembered everything he ever read. Many years later Herman Goldstine decided to test this by asking him to recite "A Tale of Two Cities." Von Neumann started on chapter one and had to be asked to stop fifteen minutes later. Budapest around 1900 produced an absurd cluster of minds: von Neumann, Eugene Wigner, Edward Teller, Leo Szilard, Paul Erdős, Theodore von Kármán, George Pólya. When several of them turned up at Los Alamos and realized they had gone to high school together, Szilard joked that Hungary was a cover story for a Martian landing. But even inside the Martian cluster , von Neumann was the outlier. Wigner, a Nobel laureate himself, was asked at Los Alamos to explain the Hungarian phenomenon and said there is only one phenomenon that is worthy of explanation, and that phenomenon is John von Neumann. The cluster may be less mysterious than it looks: Budapest was one of the few genuinely welcoming places in Europe for Jewish families, and it pushed them toward the professions the nobility considered beneath them, mathematics among them. The schools then did the rest, with a nationwide math competition and top quality high school teachers. As for the Johnny phenomenon, from the pedagogical perspective, the following stood out to me from Johnny's early years. The first is the dinner table. Von Neumann's father Miksa (Max), a lawyer turned banker so successful that the Emperor ennobled him for service to the national economy, ran the evening meal as a seminar. He would start by going through his own day: the cases he argued, the deals he negotiated, whatever was on his mind. Then each of the three boys would present on what they had been reading. The whole family would then argue about Heine's poetry, or antisemitism in Europe, or the paradoxes of omnipotence. Sometimes Max would bring home business clients, and the boys were allowed to grill them about whatever they wanted funded. Frequent guests included the director of Budapest's Theoretical Physics Institute and one of Freud's students. The second is the languages. Max knew the good times could end, told his sons so explicitly, and wanted them able to survive anywhere in any language. He was preparing them to flee. He was right. When John was fifteen, the communists took over Hungary and targeted rich families like his. A few months later the counterrevolutionaries beat the communists and then massacred thousands of Jews for supposedly collaborating. The von Neumanns survived by leaving the country at the right moments, and possibly by being too rich. Johnny's first ten years included no formal schooling at all, because organized primary schools were not a tradition there yet. He had governesses, private teachers, and his father's enormous library, and he apparently used it to memorize a 44-volume German history of the world, which he would later deploy to freak people out at parties. Finally, when he did get to the Fasori Gymnasium at eleven, the math teacher, László Rátz, concluded fairly quickly that he could not teach this kid and arranged a private tutor. The tutor was Gábor Szegő, who went on to chair the math department at Stanford. Szegő is said to have come away from the first lessons in tears at what the boy could already do. The results of this tutelage showed up a couple years later. At seventeen Johnny gave a new definition of the ordinal numbers, where each number simply is the set of all the numbers before it. Zero is the empty set. One is the set containing zero. Two is the set containing zero and one. And so on up into the infinite ordinals, with nothing but the empty set and a pair of braces to build from. If you think about it, this is a very computer-science-y way to define numbers: an inductive datatype with one constructor.  He pushed this further in his doctoral thesis a few years later. Set theory at the time was still suffering from the paradoxes, Russell's set of all sets that do not contain themselves being the famous one. Johnny's fix was essentially a type system for sets: the ordinary ones you can put inside other sets, and the oversized ones you can talk about but never use as an element. The paradox then becomes a type error. Note that it is the same abstraction move in both times: take an object everyone thinks they understand, and replace it with the smallest thing that behaves the same way. Johnny kept doing the same thing in field after field for the next thirty years: arrive, find the smallest set of objects and axioms the mess is actually about, write them down so that everyone can finally argue about the right thing, and then leave before the theorems fell out. Teller said Johnny enjoyed thinking, but I think the addiction was much more specialized than that. His real superpower was " the art of abstraction ". Look at the list from the introduction again with this in mind. Matrix mechanics and wave mechanics looked like rival theories until he noticed they were two coordinate systems on the same Hilbert space. Economists thought comparing preferences across people was hopeless until he asked what minimal consistency axioms a chooser has to satisfy, and derived a cardinal utility scale from them in an afternoon. Self-reproduction looked like it needed an infinite recursion of blueprints until he separated "read the tape as instructions" from "copy the tape as data." Making quantum mechanics rigorous Having finished his PhD at 21, Johnny arrived at Göttingen at 22 because it was the world capital of mathematics, under Hilbert. The timing couldn't have been better. Heisenberg, one year older, was down the hall having just invented matrix mechanics. A year later Schrödinger produced wave mechanics in Vienna. The two gave the same answers and implied completely different pictures of reality, and physicists were uneasy with both: matrices were unfamiliar mathematics then, and nobody could say what the waves were. Von Neumann's first move was to prove the two were the same theory in different forms. Then he wrote "Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics" (1932), which set the whole thing up rigorously in Hilbert space. The author of the book Bhattacharya, who did physics as an undergrad, points out that this is still the most watertight formulation we have.  Once the math was clean, the measurement problem became more visible. Where does the wave function actually collapse? At the apparatus, the detector, the retina, or the conscious observer? Von Neumann declined to take a position, but proved it does not matter mathematically where you draw the line because the answer comes out the same. That line is now called the von Neumann cut. Game theory and economics Nothing much came of game theory until von Neumann proved the minimax theorem in 1928, in his early twenties. Every two-player zero-sum game has a solution: either a strategy one player can pursue to win, or a mixed strategy with randomness in it (e.g., rock-paper-scissors). Then he lost interest and wandered off, as was his habit. He came back when Oskar Morgenstern turned up at Princeton. Morgenstern, an economist, was stuck on what is essentially a liveness bug in economic modeling: you intervene in an economy, people adjust their behavior in response, which invalidates the model you used to design the intervention, so you build a new model, which they also adjust to. An infinite loop. Morgenstern had concluded that all attempts to model economies must fail, which made him unpopular right up until the Wall Street crash made him look prescient. Von Neumann had the tools to attack the problem. Over about eighteen months they produced the 600-page "Theory of Games and Economic Behavior" (1944) and founded the field. Johnny did this as a hobby. During those same years he was designing implosion lenses at Los Alamos and building the first programmable computers. He would drop in on Morgenstern for a long session and then vanish back into the rest of his life. Two things from this work are still everywhere. The first is the axiomatization of expected utility. Putting human preferences on a cardinal scale and comparing them across people was considered more or less impossible, and von Neumann sat down one afternoon and did it. This relates uncomfortably with the longtermism material from the Cal Newport/Émile Torres conversation I wrote up recently . Expected value math is a hell of a drug. The second is its limited model. His framework is built on zero-sum games and on coalitions: given n players, which coalitions are stable? Most of his book is about that, but a lot of the world is not zero-sum. Nash's non-cooperative equilibrium , which generalizes minimax, is what opened that up, and von Neumann rejected it essentially out of hand when Nash walked into his office. To him it was a trivial step, a fixed-point argument he could see through instantly. He misjudged the importance of the non-cooperative approach. Bhattacharya flags a nice irony here: von Neumann, the alleged Cold War hawk and the model for Dr. Strangelove, built a theory centered on people talking to each other and forming working coalitions. It was Nash, who had trouble with people, who formalized everyone optimizing alone. All models are wrong , but some are useful. The computer In 1944 Johnny ran into Herman Goldstine on a train platform at Aberdeen, found out about the ENIAC, and attached himself to the project. In 1945 he wrote the " First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC ", laying out the stored-program architecture: one memory holding both instructions and data, a control unit, an arithmetic unit, I/O. That is now the architecture of virtually all computers, from the desktops to smartphones, eighty years later. Von Neumann was adamant that the technical details go into the public domain, and circulating that draft is exactly what made the architecture unpatentable. So Johnny was also an early proponent of Open Source. He did the same with the IAS machine design, which got copied worldwide and produced a run of machines with goofy names: MANIAC at Los Alamos, JOHNNIAC at RAND, ILLIAC at Illinois, SILLIAC in Sydney, WEIZAC in Israel. For a man who gets painted as the cold rationalist hawk, putting the foundational design of the computing industry into the commons on purpose is a generous act. He also, with Ulam, invented the Monte Carlo method , then needed random numbers for it and had to invent pseudorandom generation. And he put the first serious application on these machines himself. The IAS Meteorology Project ran the first computerized weather forecast in 1950. Numerical weather prediction, and by extension climate modeling, is a von Neumann production. Reliable organisms from unreliable components In 1952 von Neumann gave a lecture series at Caltech titled "Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components." The vacuum tubes of the day failed constantly, and the standard engineering response was to make better tubes. His response was to ask whether you could build an arbitrarily reliable machine out of components that are guaranteed to fail, using redundancy and majority voting, and then to work out how much redundancy you actually need. That is one of the founding ideas of fault-tolerant computing, and gives rise to replicated state machine, quorums, and Paxos. Self-reproducing automata In the late 1940s, Johnny started asking what it would take for a machine to build a copy of itself . The naive worry is infinite recursion: the machine needs a blueprint of itself, and that blueprint must include a blueprint of the blueprint, and so on down forever. His solution (worked out with Ulam's suggestion to set it in a discrete cellular framework) was to split the role of the description. You have a universal constructor plus a tape describing it. The constructor reads the tape as "instructions" and builds the described machine. Then it copies the tape as uninterpreted "data" and attaches the copy to the offspring. One description is used twice in two completely different modes. This is the stored-program idea again, three years after EDVAC: the same bits are instructions when you execute them and data when you copy them. He published this in 1948 and 1949. Watson and Crick published the structure of DNA in 1953. So von Neumann derived, from pure logic, the necessary architecture of biological reproduction. That there must be a stored description. That it must be read in two distinct ways. That this separation is precisely what makes open-ended evolution possible. Translation and transcription. Genotype and phenotype. He got the shape of the answer years before anyone knew what the molecule was. The 29-state cellular automaton he built to prove it was also, incidentally, the first cellular automaton. Conway's Game of Life, Wolfram's entire research program, artificial life, and a foundations of what people now call synthetic biology all descend from his formal model. "Theory of Self-Reproducing Automata" was published posthumously in 1966. His last work, also published posthumously, was "The Computer and the Brain" (1958). In it he observes that the brain achieves what it does with terrible arithmetic precision and enormous parallelism, which is the opposite of the machines he had just finished building. There he argues that whatever language the nervous system computes in, it is not mathematics as we understand mathematics. We are still working on this last one! Personality Johnny loved parties, loud music, and fast cars. He drove crowded roads like a maniac, and got bored and slowed down on open ones. He wrecked a car roughly every year, usually a Cadillac, "because no one would sell me a tank". An intersection in Princeton was christened Von Neumann Corner for the number of accidents he had there. One of his accident reports says: "I was proceeding down the road. The trees on the right were passing me in orderly fashion at 60 miles an hour. Suddenly one of them stepped in my path. Boom!" He also did his best work in chaos, and played German march music at volume in his office at Princeton, generating complaints from neighbors who included Albert Einstein. His detractors called him cold, calculating, and ruthless. He did not join the Manhattan Project colleagues who agonized afterward, and instead he pushed the government toward bigger hydrogen bombs. He advocated an immediate preemptive nuclear strike on the USSR: "If you say why not bomb them tomorrow, I say why not today? If you say today at five o'clock, I say why not one o'clock?" Very brutal. And he said it in public, more than once, to journalists, while sitting on the Atomic Energy Commission. But notice that, this is rooted in his abstraction habit. Model the Cold War as a two-player zero-sum game, assume the Soviets get the bomb soon and would use it, and minimax says strike first. The math checks out, but the problem is the very simplistic model he uses. Stanislaw Ulam, who worked beside him for twenty years, put it as kindly as it can be put: "There was perhaps an inclination to take a too exclusively rational point of view about the cases of historical events." Paradoxically, the same man was remarkably generous with people. He moved heaven and earth for those he thought were promising: Turing and Mandelbrot both benefited, and he mentored David Blackwell, a Black statistician Princeton did not want, and pushed until they took him. Blackwell wrote later about how much it mattered. Johnny put his own reputation on the line testifying for Oppenheimer, whose politics he did not share. A friend described him as "always gentle, always kind, always penetrating and always magnificently lucid." Teller said: "Von Neumann would carry on a conversation with my 3-year-old son, and the two of them would talk as equals, and I sometimes wondered if he used the same principle when he talked to the rest of us." Which brings me back to the Teller line I opened with: Johnny enjoyed thinking, and Teller suspected he enjoyed almost nothing else. That is a lovely thing to say about a man at his funeral. It is also the setup for the cruelest possible ending, and Teller knew it when he said it. The cancer, probably from the radiation he absorbed standing around at weapons tests, started in the bone and went to the brain. He had spent fifty years as the fastest mind in any room he entered, and he had to watch that go. Teller: "When [Johnny] was dying of cancer, his brain was affected. I think that he suffered from this loss more than I have seen any human to suffer in any other circumstance ". Johnny remained a game theorist to the end. After a lifetime of culturally Jewish atheism, he asked to be baptized. His daughter attributed it to Pascal's Wager: a small probability of a much better afterlife, against a trivial cost.  Can we survive technology? In 1955 von Neumann wrote an essay called "Can We Survive Technology?" He spends most of it on nuclear war, but he touches on global warming. In 1955! And a few years earlier, in a conversation Ulam recalled in his obituary, he had already coined "singularity" (yes, that singularity ) for a point where technological progress accelerates past the possibility of predicting what comes next. This is what he actually argues about whether you can solve this by banning the dangerous technology: In looking for a solution, it is well to exclude one pseudosolution at the start. The crisis will not be resolved by inhibiting this or that apparently particularly obnoxious form of technology. For one thing, the parts of technology, as well as of the underlying sciences, are so intertwined that in the long run nothing less than a total elimination of all technological progress would suffice for inhibition. He goes on to say that a ban would have to be worldwide to work, and prohibition of invention runs against the entire ethos of the industrial age, and is not going to be heeded anyways. So what does he offer instead? What safeguard remains? Apparently only day-to-day — or perhaps year-to-year — opportunistic measures, a long sequence of small, correct decisions. [...] For progress there is no cure. Any attempt to find automatically safe channels for the present explosive variety of progress must lead to frustration. The only safety possible is relative, and it lies in an intelligent exercise of day-to-day judgment. And then he names the qualities required: "patience, flexibility, intelligence". So, here is von Neumann, the master of abstraction, with no abstraction to offer. Maybe through his bout of applying minimax reasoning to nuclear strategy, he learned what a formal model is worth when the assumptions are shaky and the stakes are civilizational. book-review Get link Facebook X Pinterest Email Other Apps Comments Post a Comment Popular posts from this blog The Safest Job from AI may be Writing - August 31, 2026 Today, tech folk are scrambling to change their workflows to meet newly inflated 5X productivity quotas, while getting pummeled under the cognitive debt of agent-generated code. title: New 14‑inch MacBook Pro with M6
body_text: Apple introduces the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 - Apple (IN) Apple Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support 0 + Newsroom Open Newsroom navigation Close Newsroom navigation Apple Services Apple Stories Search Newsroom Close opens in new window PRESS RELEASE 27 October 2026 Apple introduces the new 14‑inch MacBook Pro with M6 Supercharged by M6, the 14-inch MacBook Pro features incredible performance and next-level AI capabilities, enhanced connectivity, and up to 24 hours of battery life, delivering even more value Supercharged by the all-new M6 chip, the 14-inch MacBook Pro brings extraordinary performance, AI capabilities, and up to 24 hours of battery life — making it an even more compelling value. CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 , delivering even more performance, powerful on-device AI capabilities, and faster connectivity for college students, business users, creators, and more. M6 features an advanced 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core, so everything from productivity tasks to more demanding pro workflows feels incredibly fast and responsive. 1 The 12-core GPU delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads when compared to M5, making the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 a compelling value for users who need serious power. 2 For those upgrading from M1, the performance gains are even more significant, with up to 11x faster graphics and up to 13x faster AI performance. 3 With additional Neural Accelerators in the GPU and a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, M6 turns MacBook Pro into an even more powerful platform for AI — from taking advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features across apps and macOS to running LLMs locally, all while preserving user privacy. 4 In addition, the 14-inch MacBook Pro features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, while superfast storage makes working with large files, exporting projects, and running demanding AI workflows fly. And with phenomenal battery life of up to 24 hours, it delivers the same remarkable performance whether plugged in or on battery, so users can work, create, and pursue their passions from anywhere. 3 It also offers the advanced features users love, including the stunning Liquid Retina XDR display with a nano-texture option, a 12MP Center Stage camera, an immersive six-speaker sound system, and a wide array of ports. Together with macOS 27, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is a major upgrade for existing Mac users and those coming to Mac for the first time. Available in space black and silver, it can be pre-ordered beginning tomorrow, October 28, with availability starting Friday, November 6. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 combines next-generation performance and powerful on-device AI in a portable design, empowering students, creatives, developers, and business professionals to take their workflows anywhere. “The 14-inch MacBook Pro is the pro laptop of choice for a wide range of users — from college students, to business professionals across every industry, to multidisciplinary creators doing it all on one device,” said Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With the powerful M6 chip, we’re taking performance to the next level, with a boost in CPU speed and graphics and even more powerful capabilities for on-device AI. With its amazing battery life, remarkable Liquid Retina XDR display, and even faster connectivity, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers a fantastic combination of performance, capability, and value.” M6 makes the 14-inch MacBook Pro faster than ever, thanks to a powerful 12-core CPU, advanced 12-core GPU, and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. M6: Blazing-Fast Performance and On-Device AI Capabilities M6 brings even more performance and next-level AI capabilities to the 14-inch MacBook Pro. Featuring a powerful 12-core CPU, a 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and faster unified memory, MacBook Pro with M6 is faster and more responsive. The 12-core CPU, with two more cores than before, brings blazing-fast single- and multithreaded performance, so users can fly through everything from multitasking across apps to compiling code to handling complex creative workflows. The 12-core GPU, also with two additional cores, delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance when compared to M5. 2 Everything from 3D modelling to photo editing and gaming feels incredibly fast, enhanced by a third-generation ray-tracing engine and Dynamic Caching to optimise on-chip memory. It also brings up to 25 percent faster performance for on-device AI workloads, like LLM prompt processing, compared to M5. 3 The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers up to 1.9x faster performance than M5 and works with the advanced GPU to dramatically accelerate AI workloads like image generation, Super Resolution, and AI upscaling. 2 The Neural Engine also powers Apple Intelligence, enabling advanced and energy-efficient on-device AI processing. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 does all this with industry-leading performance per watt and up to 24 hours of battery life, the longest ever in a Mac. With 16GB of unified memory standard, configurable up to 32GB, and higher memory bandwidth up to 170GB/s, MacBook Pro makes multitasking and working with demanding apps and large projects even faster. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 helps motion designers model 3D objects, design product visualisations, and render animations with ease. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 enables : 3 Up to 13x faster time to first token performance for LLM prompt processing compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5. Up to 11.7x faster render performance with ray tracing in Blender compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5. Up to 3.3x faster image-processing performance in Affinity compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.2x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5. Up to 2.5x faster project build performance when compiling code in Xcode compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5. A project is edited in Adobe After Effects on a 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. An image is edited in the Pixelmator Pro app on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. Lines of code are compiled in Xcode on the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. Film editors and content creators can quickly and efficiently composite visual effects and add cinematic motion graphics in popular video editing tools on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. Photographers and designers can make complex AI-powered image adjustments in real time using apps like Pixelmator Pro on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. Developers can build and test their apps with blazing-fast compile times in Xcode on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. previous next A Huge Upgrade with Even More Value There’s never been a better time for customers to upgrade from a previous-generation MacBook Pro with Apple silicon or an Intel-based Mac. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers remarkable value thanks to major performance improvements and powerful AI capabilities. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro also features all of the compelling capabilities that have made it so popular, including: Phenomenal battery life : In addition to the huge leap in performance, battery life gets up to 14 additional hours for Intel-based upgraders and up to four more hours for users coming from M1, delivering up to 24 hours overall, so users can get more done on a single charge. Users coming from Intel-based and M1 systems will also get 16GB of starting unified memory, an additional Thunderbolt port, and the space black finish with an anodisation seal for fewer fingerprints. A brilliant pro display : The stunning Liquid Retina XDR display delivers up to 1600 nits of peak HDR brightness and a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio, bringing HDR photos and videos to life with deep blacks, brilliant highlights, and vibrant colours. And for users working in bright or challenging lighting conditions, a nano-texture display option dramatically reduces reflections and glare. Powerful connectivity : Now with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, the 14-inch MacBook Pro delivers fast wireless performance and low latency, along with support for up to two external displays. Its versatile array of ports — including the HDMI, MagSafe 3, and three Thunderbolt 4 ports; an SDXC card slot; and a headphone jack — makes it easy to connect high-speed peripherals, transfer photos, or expand a workspace. Advanced camera, mics, and speakers : A 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View helps keep users perfectly framed on video calls, while a studio-quality three-mic array and amazing six-speaker sound system with Spatial Audio deliver an immersive audio experience. Fast charging : MacBook Pro with M6 supports fast charging, reaching up to 50 percent charge in just 30 minutes when paired with a compatible higher-wattage USB-C power adapter, such as the 96W Power Adapter. 3 A laptop that’s built to last : With an enclosure made from 100 percent recycled aluminium, MacBook Pro is exceptionally durable and can stand up to everyday use for years to come. Better together with iPhone : When used together with Continuity, iPhone and Mac are even more powerful — letting users move seamlessly across devices to share files and photos, hand off tasks, and even control their iPhone from their 14-inch MacBook Pro. 5 Users switching to Mac for the first time can use iPhone to conveniently and securely transfer settings, files, photos, passwords, and more. The Liquid Retina XDR display is showcased on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6. Two sides of the new 14-inch MacBook Pro show the laptop’s array of ports. The brilliant Liquid Retina XDR display delivers up to 1600 nits of peak HDR brightness and a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio. HDR photos and videos look more true to life with deep blacks, brilliant highlights, and vibrant colours. With the new 14-inch MacBook Pro, users can connect high-speed peripherals, transfer photos, work with multiple external displays, and more with its wide array of ports. previous next macOS 27 Golden Gate The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 comes to life with macOS 27, which includes Siri AI, a profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal assistant; helpful Apple Intelligence features across everyday apps; and improvements that make the Mac even more responsive and reliable. Siri AI can draw on personal context to help users find what they need in the moment across messages, emails, photos, and more; answer questions about virtually any topic; and get things done across apps — all with groundbreaking privacy protections. Siri AI is integrated into Spotlight and systemwide context menus, and users can ask Siri about what’s on their display with Visual Intelligence using a dedicated keyboard shortcut. Users can also write and edit with Siri almost anywhere they type. Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful. In Safari, it powers new tools that automatically organise a user’s tabs into topics; notify them of website changes, like product restocks or price drops; and enable the creation of custom extensions based on a description. Users can also easily create an automation in Shortcuts by simply describing it, or tap into intelligent photo editing tools in the Photos app. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro gets even more responsive, reliable, and delightful with refinements to design, performance, search, and more. Updates to Liquid Glass deliver an even more focused and approachable experience. A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalise Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference, and app icons are sharper and more defined. 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 and the Environment The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 45 percent recycled content overall, 6 including 100 percent recycled aluminium in the enclosure, 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery, and, in a first for Apple, 100 percent recycled tantalum in multiple capacitors. It is manufactured with 60 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is designed to be durable and repairable, and meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based 7 and designed to be recycled. Pricing and Availability Customers can pre-order the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starting tomorrow, October 28, on apple.com/in/store and in the Apple Store app in 35 countries and regions, including the U.S. It will begin arriving to customers, and in Apple Store locations and Apple Authorized Resellers, starting Friday, November 6. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at INR 239900 and INR 227900 with education savings . Additional technical specifications and configure-to-order options are available at apple.com/in/macbook-pro . Details on Apple accessories — including the 70W Power Adapter for INR 5800 , 96W Power Adapter for INR 8900 , 140W Power Adapter for INR 11900 , and the World Travel Adapter Kit for INR 4900 — are available at apple.com/in/mac . With Apple Trade In, customers can trade in their current computer and get credit toward a new Mac. Customers can visit apple.com/in/shop/trade-in to see what their device is worth. With year-round education pricing — available to current and newly accepted college students and educators — customers can save on MacBook Pro, along with a wide range of products and services through the Apple Store online and in stores. Visit the Apple Education Store for details. AppleCare delivers exceptional service and support, with flexible options for Apple users. Customers can choose AppleCare+ to cover their new Mac or, in available markets, AppleCare One to protect multiple products in one simple plan. Both plans include coverage for accidents like drops and spills, theft and loss protection on eligible products, battery replacement service, and priority support from Apple Experts. For more information, visit apple.com/in/applecare . Every customer who buys directly from Apple gets access to Personal Setup. In these guided one-on-one online sessions, a Specialist can walk them through setup or focus on features that will help them make the most of their new device. Customers can also learn more about getting started and going further with their new device with a Today at Apple session at their nearest Apple Store.
